title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
text:
Israeli consumer-price inflation peaked at 463 percent year-over-year in Q4 1984 (Chart 1). In mid-1985, inflation stood at above 12 percent a month, or about 290 percent annualized.1 The economy’s foreign exchange reserves were quickly falling, as Israel experienced capital flight.2 To improve the situation, a national-unity government led by Prime Minister Shimon Peres launched an emergency stabilization plan on July 1, 1985.3 The plan effectively ended the macroeconomic crisis: within a few months, monthly inflation fell to 1 to 2 percent, reserves were rising, and unemployment rose by only about two percentage points. This has since been hailed as a successful model of rapid disinflation. My thesis is that the crisis was not caused by a large deficit alone: indexing wages, assets, and the exchange rate to past prices turned a persistent fiscal imbalance and a financial shock into near-hyperinflation, which is why only a combined fiscal and exchange-rate reform could end it.
This blog post analyzes five key macroeconomic indicators to show how Israel got to the point of crisis, how it nearly lost control, and why the stabilization plan worked. Each chart answers the next question in the chain: how fast did prices run away, why was the economy so vulnerable, how did Israelis react, why did output hold up, and how was the situation eventually handled? Throughout, I use the metaphor of a fire: the budget deficit is the tinder, a bank-share collapse the spark, and indexation the accelerant. To end the crisis, Israel had to fix the government budget and re-anchor prices.
All charts are interactive: hover over them to see the precise values at each point, which lets you match the charts to the textual analysis. The charts were built using R with Quarto. The datasets used are available along the right pane of this website.

title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
section: A Ratchet That Only Turned Up
text:
A Ratchet That Only Turned Up






Chart 1
Source: OECD via FRED.
Series: ISRCPALTT01IXNBQ.
Measure: quarterly CPI, % change vs. the same quarter a year earlier.
Shaded area: 1983–85 (Crisis Period).
Dashed line: July 1985 stabilization plan.
Chart 1 above shows year-over-year CPI inflation. In the run-up to the crisis, inflation increased in steps, such as in 1973–74, 1977, 1979, and 1983–84. After each jump, it settled onto a new plateau.4 From 1980 to 1983, it hovered between 104 and 136 percent. Then it rose rapidly: from 126 percent in Q3 1983 to 175 percent in Q4 1983, peaking at 463 percent in Q4 1984.
After the crisis, inflation ended sharply. After the July 1985 stabilization plan, it fell from 379 percent in the third quarter of 1985 to 211 percent in the fourth. By Q3 1986, it had fallen to just 21 percent. Despite this, inflation stayed between 15 and 22 percent until early 1992 and dropped below 8 percent only in late 1995.
The answer to why inflation ratcheted upwards lies in the analysis of Michael Bruno, the Israeli economist who helped lead the July 1985 stabilization effort. Bruno stated that Israel was an economy in which liquid financial assets were linked to prices or to the U.S. dollar. Therefore, the exchange rate adjusted roughly in line with past inflation, and wage agreements adjusted for price increases monthly.5 Price shocks, such as currency devaluations or subsidy cuts, were passed into wages, assets, and the exchange rate, which produced higher inflation. But indexation was the accelerant, something that helped the crisis spread, rather than the fire itself. To find the tinder, we have to look at the government’s balance sheet.

title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
text:
The Tinder and the Spark







  
    
    Excluding interest
  
  
    
    Including interest
  

Chart 2
Source: Bruno (1986), Table 2, citing Bank of Israel Research Department and the Accountant General’s Office.
Measure: domestic government deficit, % of GDP, excluding and including interest. Fiscal years run April–March.
Note: The two right-hand pairs compare April–November 1984 with April–November 1985. They are partial periods, not full-year figures; Bruno reports only these months for those years. Bruno’s estimates do not correct for the inflationary erosion of unindexed loans to the private sector, which he puts at an additional 5–8 percent of GDP in 1978–82 and 1–2 percent in 1983–84.
A textbook explanation of very high inflation, associated with Milton Friedman’s monetarism, points to a large deficit financed by money creation.6 In Israel’s case, the deficit was large, but the relationship was not that simple. Bruno describes the deficit as “more or less stable” at 12 to 15 percent of GDP while inflation leapt from 30 to 40 percent in 1973–76 to nearly 500 percent annualized in 1984–85.7 Chart 2 draws on his Table 2: the deficit including interest ranged from 8 to 15 percent of GDP in 1977–84, mostly near 9 percent, and it was no larger in 1983 than in 1979–80. Therefore, the deficit alone does not explain why inflation exploded in 1983–84.
Chart 2 does show a drastic improvement in 1985: the deficit including interest fell from 15 percent of GDP in April–November 1984 to 6 percent in the same months of 1985. The roots of the deficit go back to 1973, when Israel fought the Yom Kippur War. Although it emerged victorious militarily, the war was followed by slower growth, soaring military expenditures, and national trauma.8 Investment was falling and there was growing dependence on foreign borrowing.9 A decade of public spending beyond what the economy had produced meant that government debt stood at 284 percent of GDP.10 This was, at the time, one of the highest ratios in the world.11 Simultaneously, the share of employment in the public sector had grown from 20 to 30 percent over the decade.12
The large deficit also widened the balance-of-payments gap, leading to repeated devaluations and subsidy cuts, which in turn pushed prices up. Further, by 1984, real gross wages were about 16 percent above their 1980 level, while output per worker remained stagnant.13 Spending raced ahead of what the economy could sustain.14
A financial shock lit the fuse. For years, Israel’s banks had been artificially propping up their own share prices by lending to clients and buying back their own shares, creating an illusion of steady demand.15 Government-supported bank shares became one of the liquid assets that kept pace with inflation.16 In October 1983, this system collapsed, and a large devaluation followed in the same quarter. In Israel, this was known as “Black Thursday”: the Tel Aviv stock exchange was forced to close for 18 days.17 The 1983 jump in inflation came in the fourth quarter, after both the bank-share crisis and the devaluation, as Chart 1 shows. Once the fire was lit, Israelis moved their savings out of the shekel.

title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
text:
Running from the Shekel






Chart 3
Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators.
Series: FI.RES.XGLD.CD.
Measure: Total reserves minus gold (current US$).
Shaded area: 1983–85 (Crisis Period).
A currency comes under pressure when the country is running out of foreign money. Chart 3 shows this pressure building for Israel. Foreign exchange reserves (excluding gold) fell by about 18 percent between 1982 and 1984, from $3.8 billion to $3.1 billion. (The series counts the assets a central bank can deploy directly, such as foreign exchange holdings, special drawing rights, and the IMF reserve position, and leaves out gold.)18
In Israel’s case, reserves fell even as the trade balance improved. The Israeli economy underwent capital flight: Israelis lost faith in the government’s ability to restrain prices and bought dollars in large amounts.19 By 1983–84, the country’s short-term foreign debts exceeded its reserves, a warning sign also seen before the 1982 Latin American debt crisis.20
The loss of confidence also affected interest rates. On the eve of the stabilization plan, dollar-linked assets earned an effective 17 percent per month in interest when measured in Israeli shekels. Immediately after the plan, that number fell to 3 percent.21 This indicated that the plan successfully convinced people that the shekel would hold its value, dissipating the incentive to flee.22 Reserves rose about 20 percent in 1985, kept rising for a few years, and fell again in 1988. But the fire did not burn the real economy.

title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
text:
The Growth Paradox






Chart 4
Source: Penn World Table (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015) via FRED, series RGDPNAILA666NRUG.
Measure: real GDP at constant national prices, Israel.
Note: growth rates calculated by the author from year-over-year changes in the level.
Unlike most inflation crises, the Israeli crisis was not accompanied by an economic collapse. Chart 4 shows that Israeli real GDP growth never turned negative in the crisis years: it was 3.4 percent in 1983, 0.9 percent in 1984, and 4.0 percent in 1985. Here, the Penn World Table is used because it gives one consistent real-GDP series for 1972–1995, and growth rates are calculated from its levels.23 Growth then recovered, at 4.2 percent in 1986 and 7.1 percent in 1987, though unevenly: it fell to 0.6 percent in 1989.
Output held up, yet instability persisted. MERIP reported at the time that inflation had virtually broken the statistical system that decision makers relied on to forecast and plan, and that firms and financial institutions were overreacting by shifting into dollar-linked assets.24 In practice, shorter planning horizons and the constant cost of adjusting prices and wages were the real price of the crisis. Even so, instability was rampant, and by mid-1985 the first attempt at dousing the fire had failed.

title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
text:
Putting Out the Fire






Chart 5
Source: OECD via FRED, series CCUSMA02ILM618N.
Measure: new Israeli shekels per US dollar, monthly average.
Note: log scale, so equal percentage changes look equal across the whole period.
Shaded area: 1983–85 (Crisis Period).
Dashed line: July 1985 stabilization plan; the shekel was pegged to the US dollar.
Initially, Israel tried to stabilize gradually. Between late 1984 and mid-1985, the government negotiated “package deals” with unions and employers that froze prices and set planned wage increases.25 But since these provisions were not accompanied by appropriate budget cuts and the shekel kept being devalued, the attempt was largely unsuccessful.26 A price freeze does not work if the exchange rate keeps moving, since persistent currency fluctuations trigger product shortages, uncertainty, and black markets. By June 1985, the situation had deteriorated enough to rule out a gradual solution.
Instead, the government launched a rapid stabilization plan that attacked both causes of the crisis at once.27 Fiscally, it announced a $1.5 billion cut in the budget deficit,28 about 7.5 percent of GDP, mostly through subsidy cuts and taxes, along with a planned 3 percent cut in public employment.29 Chart 2 shows the result: the deficit including interest fell from 15 to 6 percent of GDP between April–November 1984 and the same months of 1985. On the nominal side, Israel devalued the shekel by 18.8 percent and then pegged it to the dollar.30 It also froze wages, prices, and credit.31 The Histadrut, Israel’s largest labor federation, agreed to a temporary suspension of cost-of-living adjustments in exchange for immediate compensation of 14 percent of wages.32 The United States also came to Israel’s aid, supporting the plan with $750 million in emergency aid in 1985 and 1986.33 On the other hand, the fiscal cut was less than ideal: political leaders ruled out cuts to the defense budget, so the reduction ended up being $1.5 billion34 rather than the $2 to $2.5 billion required to prevent the growth of government debt.35
The exchange rate adjustment, together with the matching freeze in nominal wages and price controls, completed the stabilization plan. The controls were eventually lifted from January 1986 as the economy recovered.36 Yet, stabilization also carried a modest cost. Average real gross wages fell by about 14 percent between fiscal year 1984 and 1985, unemployment rose by two percentage points, and real interest rates stayed high for months.37
Chart 5 shows the shekel’s path and is the litmus test for the plan. Between January 1983 and July 1985, the shekel lost value about forty-three-fold against the dollar, from about 0.035 to 1.49 new shekels per dollar. Over 1972 to July 1985 the rate rose about 3,500-fold (from 0.00042), and by December 1995 it stood at 3.12, about 7,400 times its 1972 level. (A log scale is used because it makes equal percentage changes look equal; on a linear scale, everything before the early 1980s would look flat.) In 1985–86, Israel replaced the old shekel with the new shekel at a rate of 1,000 old shekels to 1 new shekel, which removed three zeros from prices and wages.38 The series is expressed in new shekels throughout, so the redenomination does not distort it. After July 1985, the line went flat: the rate stood at 1.49 in both January and July 1986. Once the shekel was pegged, the accelerant was gone: past prices no longer fed wages, assets, and the exchange rate.

title: Israel’s 1983–1985 Inflation Crisis
section: What We Can Learn From This
text:
What We Can Learn From This

The crisis required a coordinated fiscal and monetary response. The deficit was a long-term problem, but the inflation was driven by the way the system amplified shocks. Freezing prices without fiscal reform was not feasible, and fixing the budget without freezing wages and the exchange rate did not work either.
Credibility matters. The gradual process attempted first asked the public to believe in a slow, drawn-out process. In the end, a sudden, comprehensive plan backed by the government, unions, and employers worked by changing expectations quickly, as the collapse in dollar interest rates shows.
The plan was a start to the recovery, not the whole of it. It was helped by external aid, and most of its budgetary cuts came from subsidy cuts and taxes rather than reduced direct government activity.39 Inflation remained at 15 to 22 percent for years, and lasting success depended on budget restraint and wage moderation. By stopping the crisis, the plan may have helped create the conditions for growth in the 1990s,40 but the early-1990s wave of immigration confounded the causes of growth, so the plan cannot take the credit for that growth alone.41
Finally, there is value in thinking through the political lens. In my reading, Israel’s high inflation was fixed by a political coalition of government, unions, and employers that agreed to share the pain for the country’s future, rather than by a specific economic ideology.42
